features.doc: The repeated description of a ch. 9 sloppy-identity row, bare or carrying a bound relation.

examples.primaryText: The cat grins.
paperFeatures: [[[the cat] s1] grins] or [ς1 [[[the cat] s1] grins]]
examples.comment: Two analyses: a referential situation pronoun discharges the uniqueness condition at its referent, a bound one carries it to the topic situation by λ-Conversion II.

examples.primaryText: The murderer is insane.
examples.context: Attributive: Smith is found foully murdered and no one knows by whom. Referential: Jones is on trial for the murder and behaving oddly in court.
examples.comment: The referential use has a situation pronoun referring to the courtroom; the attributive use has it bound, so the description is evaluated at the topic situation. Elbourne's (2) alters Donnellan's 'Smith's murderer is insane' (ch. 5, (1)), dropping the Saxon genitive.

examples.primaryText: Who is the man drinking a martini?
examples.context: The man gestured at is drinking water from a martini glass.
examples.comment: Misdescription: a question about a particular person is asked, and the Fregean account locates what went wrong in a false presupposition of existence.

examples.primaryText: Scott is the author of Waverley.
examples.comment: Predicative use is attributive use: the bound description gives a proposition false at situations where someone else authored Waverley, unlike the identity statement.

examples.primaryText: Every man who owns a donkey beats the donkey.
examples.comment: The description's situation pronoun is bound by σ to the minimal situations of the restrictor, each of which contains exactly one donkey.

examples.primaryText: If a man beats a donkey, the donkey always kicks him.

contrasts.form: If a man beats a donkey, the donkey kicks him.

paperFeatures: donkey-anaphoric definite description under a quantificational adverb
examples.comment: The quantificational adverb quantifies over minimal situations in which a man beats a donkey; both descriptions are bound to those situations.

examples.primaryText: John fed no cat of Mary's before the cat was bathed.
examples.comment: The covarying description in the scope of the quantifier is bound by the same mechanism as a donkey description.

examples.primaryText: Mary believes that the man who lives upstairs is a spy.
paperFeatures: situation pronoun referring to the actual world
examples.comment: De dicto: every doxastic alternative contains exactly one man upstairs. De re: the man upstairs in the actual world need not live upstairs in Mary's alternatives.

examples.primaryText: The number of the planets is necessarily odd.
examples.context: The speaker does not know how many planets there are, but astronomical theory dictates that the number is odd.
examples.comment: Attributive yet de re: the description is bound by a binder above the modal, so the number is fixed in the topic situation and oddness is claimed in every accessible world. Elbourne's (16) simplifies Kripke's 'The number of planets (whatever it may be) is necessarily odd' (ch. 7, (15)), dropping the parenthetical and adding 'the'.

examples.primaryText: Hans wants the ghost in his attic to be quiet tonight.

contrasts.form: Hans wants there to be exactly one ghost in his attic and for it to be quiet tonight.

paperFeatures: Hans believes there is exactly one ghost in his attic
examples.comment: The Russellian paraphrase (7), printed unmarked, attributes to Hans the desire to have a ghost, a reading (3) lacks; the Fregean analysis presupposes that Hans believes there is exactly one.

examples.primaryText: If the ghost in his attic is quiet tonight, Hans will hold a party.
paperFeatures: there is exactly one ghost in Hans's attic
examples.comment: The antecedent of a conditional is a hole: the existence presupposition projects to the whole sentence.

examples.primaryText: I do not know whether there are any ghosts in Hans's attic. But if the ghost in his attic is quiet tonight, he will hold a party.
discourseSegments: I do not know whether there are any ghosts in Hans's attic.
But if the ghost in his attic is quiet tonight, he will hold a party.

contrasts.form: I do not know whether there are any ghosts in Hans's attic. But if there is exactly one ghost in his attic and it is quiet tonight, he will hold a party.

paperFeatures: definite description against its Russellian paraphrase
examples.comment: Printed unmarked; native speakers judge that the speaker of (22) sounds self-contradictory but the speaker of the Russellian paraphrase (23) does not, so the paraphrase cannot be accurate.

examples.primaryText: I am unsure whether there is a ghost in my attic. I would like the ghost in my attic to be quiet tonight.
discourseSegments: I am unsure whether there is a ghost in my attic.
I would like the ghost in my attic to be quiet tonight.

contrasts.form: I am unsure whether there is a ghost in my attic. I would like there to be an entity such that it is a ghost in my attic and nothing else is a ghost in my attic and it is quiet tonight.

paperFeatures: definite description against its Russellian paraphrase under an attitude verb
examples.comment: Printed unmarked; native speakers judge Hans's attitudes inconsistent if (31) is followed by (33b) and consistent if followed by the Russellian paraphrase (33a): the description presupposes that he believes there is exactly one ghost.

examples.primaryText: Ponce de León is wondering whether the fountain of youth is in Florida.
examples.context: The speaker does not believe in the existence of a fountain of youth.

readings.name: no speaker commitment to a fountain of youth

paperFeatures: Ponce de León believes there is exactly one fountain of youth
examples.comment: The description under the attitude verb commits the subject, not the speaker, to the existence of a fountain of youth.

examples.primaryText: The table is covered with books.
examples.context: Said in a room containing exactly one table, in a world containing many.
paperFeatures: situation pronoun referring to the room
examples.comment: An incomplete description: the uniqueness condition is relativized to the restrictor situation contributed by the situation pronoun.

examples.primaryText: In this village, if a farmer owns a donkey, he beats the donkey and the priest beats the donkey too.
examples.context: The final verb phrase is downstressed.
examples.comment: No sloppy reading: the priest is not said to beat his own donkey. A situation pronoun in the final description cannot covary with the priest.

examples.primaryText: In this village, if a farmer owns a donkey, he beats the donkey he owns and the priest beats the donkey he owns too.
examples.context: The final verb phrase is downstressed.
examples.comment: With an overt bound pronoun in the description the sloppy reading is available, as relation-variable theories predict for (17a) too, wrongly.

examples.primaryText: Every man who owns a donkey beats it.
examples.comment: The donkey pronoun is the definite article with a deleted NP; its LF and meaning are those of the description in ch. 6, (3).

examples.primaryText: I saw the Junior Dean. He was worried about the Bollinger dinner.
discourseSegments: He was worried about the Bollinger dinner.
examples.comment: A referential pronoun with a deleted NP recovered from its linguistic antecedent.

examples.primaryText: He is usually an Italian.
examples.context: Said while pointing at Benedict XVI.

contrasts.form: Benedict XVI is usually an Italian.

examples.comment: A descriptive indexical: the pronoun is the article with the NP Pope, and usually quantifies over papal reigns. (35), printed unmarked, cannot have the meaning of (34).

examples.primaryText: He Who Must Not Be Named

contrasts.form: It which rolls fastest gathers no moss.

examples.comment: A Voldemort phrase: the pronoun combines with a restrictive relative clause on a silent NP person, so pronouns form definite descriptions in the open.
